title: 4 Bib Gourmand Soup Spots in Seoul You Can Just Walk Into
html:
If the weather in Seoul has turned cold and you want something warm, filling, and not spicy, you are looking for gomtang (곰탕) and its cousin seolleongtang (설렁탕) — milky-white Korean soups made by slow-boiling beef or chicken bones for hours. They taste mild and comforting, almost like a very good homemade broth, which makes them one of the easiest Korean dishes for a first-time visitor to order with zero fear of a spicy surprise. Below are four restaurants that all hold a MICHELIN Guide Seoul Bib Gourmand award (Michelin's pick for excellent, affordable food) — and all four are walk-in spots, so you don't need to book ahead in Korean to eat well.

Kyewol Gomtang (계월) — Chicken Bone Broth in Seongsu-dong

Most gomtang is made with beef, but Kyewol Gomtang specializes in dak-gomtang (닭곰탕) — the same slow-simmered idea, but with chicken. It's an even lighter, gentler bowl than the beef version, which makes it a great first soup if you're easing into Korean food. The restaurant sits in trendy Seongsu-dong, a short walk from Seongsu Station (Line 2), so you can easily pair lunch here with an afternoon exploring the neighborhood's cafes and shops.

The menu is deliberately tiny — just a few chicken-based dishes, including a cold noodle option in warmer months — and seating is mostly at a counter, so solo travelers will feel right at home. Hours run roughly 11:00–14:30 and 17:00–20:30, and the restaurant is believed to close on public holidays, so it's worth a quick phone or map-app check on the day you plan to go. Credit cards are accepted.

Hapjeongok (합정옥) — A Family's Beef Bone Soup Recipe Near Hapjeong Station

Hapjeongok is the classic version of gomtang: a deep, beef bone broth recipe that the restaurant says started as a family's own kitchen tradition. You'll find it on the 2nd floor, 21 Yanghwa-ro 1-gil, Mapo-gu — about a minute's walk from Hapjeong Station (Lines 2 and 6, Exit 5), making it one of the easier Bib Gourmand restaurants in Seoul to reach without a taxi.

It's open daily from 11:00 to 22:00, which is a long window compared to many Korean restaurants that close between lunch and dinner — handy if your sightseeing schedule runs late or you just get hungry at an odd hour. Like most gomtang shops, the broth itself is only lightly seasoned when it arrives; you'll season it yourself at the table (more on that below).

Mapo Ok (마포옥) — Seoul's Seolleongtang Institution Since 1949

Mapo Ok has been serving seolleongtang — a close relative of gomtang, usually made with ox bones and served with thin slices of beef and glass noodles — since 1949, which makes it one of the older continuously-running soup restaurants in the city. It's located at 312 Tojeong-ro, Mapo-gu, about a 3-minute walk from Mapo Station (Line 5, Exit 1).

Because Hapjeongok and Mapo Ok are both in Mapo-gu and only a short subway ride apart, they're easy to combine into a one-day "soup crawl" if you want to compare beef gomtang and seolleongtang side by side. Mapo Ok keeps early, breakfast-friendly hours: 07:00–21:00 on weekdays and 07:00–17:00 on weekends — a good option if you're jet-lagged and wide awake before the rest of Seoul opens for the day.

Neungdong Minari (능동미나리) — A Newer Favorite Worth the Short Wait

The newest Bib Gourmand pick of the four, Neungdong Minari (Sinyongsan branch) earned its award in 2025 for a rich, collagen-heavy beef bone soup. It's at 28 Hangang-daero 40-gil, Yongsan-gu, within walking distance of Sinyongsan Station (Line 4) and Samgakji Station. A fun, unusual detail for a soup restaurant: it also offers natural wine and sake if you want a drink alongside your bowl.

It's open 11:00–23:00 (last order 21:50) and does not take reservations through official channels, so expect to line up a little, especially around lunch and dinner peaks — some branches limit the soup to a set number of bowls per day, so going earlier rather than later is the safer bet.

How Koreans Actually Eat Gomtang and Seolleongtang

One thing that surprises a lot of first-time visitors: the broth usually arrives almost unsalted. That's on purpose. Koreans season their own bowl at the table, usually with a spoonful of salt and chopped green onion provided alongside, and often add a splash of kimchi brine (the liquid at the bottom of a kimchi container) for extra tang — Mapo Ok's staff will even bring you some if you ask. Don't be shy about adding more than you think you need; a perfectly seasoned bowl is saltier than most people expect on the first try. Pair your soup with kkakdugi (깍두기, cubed radish kimchi) on the side — locals almost always order it together with these soups, and its crunch is the perfect contrast to the soft broth.

💬 Tried one of these soup spots, or planning to? Tell us which one in the comments — we'd love to hear how your bowl turned out!

meta_description: 4 Bib Gourmand bone-broth soup spots in Seoul for first-time visitors — mild, budget-friendly, walk-in only. Perfect for a cold day.
